title: TensorFlow: Shapes & Layers
blurb: Do the layer arithmetic in your head: Dense kernels, the conv output formula, and the fate of the time axis in stacked RNNs.

cells.title: Dense: a matrix multiply on the last axis
cells.body:
A Dense layer is one matrix multiply plus a bias: output = input @ W + b, with W of shape (in_features, units) and b of shape (units,). Two facts fall out immediately. The output's last axis becomes units — every other axis (the batch axis, a time axis) passes through untouched. And the parameter count is always in_features × units + units: one weight per (input, output) pair, plus one bias per output unit.

This is why shape reasoning is pure arithmetic: see Dense(32) after an input of width 16 and you can compute the kernel (16 × 32 = 512 weights), the bias (32), the total (544) and the output shape (…, 32) without instantiating anything. Forgetting the bias is the most common slip — the bias counts once per output unit, not per input feature.

demo.code:
def dense_params(in_features, units):
    return in_features * units + units      # kernel + bias

print('Dense(3) on (None, 4):')
print('  output shape: (None, 3)')
print('  params: 4*3 + 3 =', dense_params(4, 3))
print('Dense(5) on (None, 12): params: 12*5 + 5 =', dense_params(12, 5))

cells.title: Convolution and pooling arithmetic
cells.body:
Convolution and pooling sizes follow one formula each, and both are worth memorizing. For a conv layer: out = (H − K + 2P) / S + 1 — input height H, kernel K, padding P, stride S. padding='valid' means P = 0 (no padding at all); padding='same' means pad just enough to keep the spatial size (for a kernel of 3, that is P = 1 on every side). The channel axis obeys a different rule: it becomes the number of filters, regardless of the input depth — each filter learns a kernel of K × K × in_channels.

MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2) takes the max over each 2×2 window, and its stride defaults to the pool size — so it simply halves H and W (28 becomes 14) and leaves the channel count alone. Whenever you review a CNN, run the formula layer by layer; it is faster than any debugger.

demo.code:
def conv_out(H, K, pad=0, stride=1):
    return (H - K + 2 * pad) // stride + 1

print('28x28 image, kernel 3:')
print('  valid (pad 0):', conv_out(28, 3))
print('  same  (pad 1):', conv_out(28, 3, pad=1))
print('  pad 2        :', conv_out(28, 3, pad=2))
print("then 2x2 pool (stride 2) on the 'same' result:",
      conv_out(conv_out(28, 3, pad=1), 2, stride=2))

cells.title: Recurrent layers keep or drop the time axis
cells.body:
Recurrent layers have a switch that decides the fate of the time axis. LSTM(units, return_sequences=True) returns the hidden state at every timestep: shape (batch, timesteps, units). With return_sequences=False (the default) it returns only the last timestep's hidden state: shape (batch, units) — the whole sequence collapses to a single vector.

The stacking rule that follows: every recurrent layer feeding another recurrent layer must set return_sequences=True, because the next layer expects a 3-D sequence, not a 2-D vector; only the last recurrent layer (or one feeding a plain Dense head) may drop the sequences. And remember from the Dense concept: Dense only ever remaps the last axis, so applying it to (batch, T, units) keeps T and maps units to its own width — one transformation per timestep.

exercise.title: Predict: one Dense layer
exercise.statement: Warm up your layer arithmetic. This model has exactly one Dense layer on top of an input of width 10. Predict the two printed values — the output shape and the total parameter count.
exercise.code:
from tensorflow.keras import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense, Input

model = Sequential([
    Input(shape=(10,)),
    Dense(64),
])
print(model.output_shape)
print(model.count_params())
exercise.explain: Dense computes input @ W + b with kernel W shaped (10, 64) and bias b shaped (64,). The last axis is remapped from 10 to 64, and the batch axis stays None — so the output shape is (None, 64). Parameters: 10 × 64 = 640 weights plus 64 bias terms = 704. B forgets the bias entirely; C counts only 10 biases — one per input feature — but there is one bias per output unit, which is 64; D keeps the input width, but Dense always remaps the last axis to its unit count. Note that the batch dimension never contributes parameters: None in a shape is about layout, not learnable sizes.

exercise.title: Predict: Flatten then Dense
exercise.statement: A classic MNIST-shaped head. The model flattens a 28×28 image and maps it to 10 logits. Predict the two printed values — and watch out for the trap hidden in one of the options, which describes a model that would run without any error.
exercise.code:
from tensorflow.keras import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense, Flatten, Input

model = Sequential([
    Input(shape=(28, 28)),
    Flatten(),
    Dense(10),
])
print(model.output_shape)
print(model.count_params())
exercise.explain: Flatten rolls the 28 × 28 grid into a single axis of 28 × 28 = 784 values, giving (None, 784). Dense(10) then uses a kernel of shape (784, 10) — 7,840 weights — plus 10 biases = 7,850 parameters, and the output is (None, 10). A is the forgot-the-bias slip again (7,840 + 10 = 7,850). C stops at the Flatten output and imagines one parameter per input value. D is the interesting trap: it is what you would get without the Flatten — Dense remaps only the last axis, so on (None, 28, 28) it would map each row of 28 features to 10, giving (None, 28, 10) with kernel (28, 10) plus 10 biases = 290 parameters. That wrong model builds and trains without any error — it is just semantically wrong, which is exactly why this prediction skill matters.

exercise.title: Predict: Conv2D then MaxPooling2D
exercise.statement: CNN shape arithmetic with a twist: the same two-layer model is built twice, once with padding='same' and once with padding='valid'. Predict both printed lines — the output shape after conv plus pooling, for each padding mode.
exercise.code:
from tensorflow.keras import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Conv2D, Input, MaxPooling2D

def build(padding):
    return Sequential([
        Input(shape=(32, 32, 3)),
        Conv2D(32, kernel_size=3, padding=padding, activation='relu'),
        MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2),
    ])

for padding in ('same', 'valid'):
    m = build(padding)
    print(padding, '->', m.output_shape)
exercise.explain: Use out = (H − K + 2P)/S + 1. With padding='same' and kernel 3, P = 1: (32 − 3 + 2×1)/1 + 1 = 32, so the conv output is (32, 32, 32) — spatial size preserved, channels equal to the number of filters. MaxPooling2D(2) has stride defaulting to the pool size, so it halves each spatial dim: 32/2 = 16, giving (None, 16, 16, 32). With padding='valid', P = 0: (32 − 3)/1 + 1 = 30, so (30, 30, 32), and pooling gives 30/2 = 15: (None, 15, 15, 32). B forgets that 'same' zero-pads precisely to preserve the size; C subtracts the pool size (30 − 2 = 28) instead of dividing — pooling with size 2 and stride 2 halves, it does not shave; D keeps the input's 3 channels, but the channel axis is always replaced by the filter count (here 32 filters, each holding a 3×3×3 kernel: 3·3·3·32 + 32 = 896 weights and biases).

exercise.title: Predict: a stacked LSTM model
exercise.statement: The final shape puzzle: a stacked LSTM model reading sequences of 20 timesteps with 8 features per step. Three layers, three printed shapes. Predict all three — the fate of the time axis is the whole game.
exercise.code:
from tensorflow.keras import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense, Input, LSTM

model = Sequential([
    Input(shape=(20, 8)),            # 20 timesteps, 8 features per step
    LSTM(64, return_sequences=True),
    LSTM(32),
    Dense(10),
])
print(model.layers[0].output_shape)  # LSTM(64, return_sequences=True)
print(model.layers[1].output_shape)  # LSTM(32)
print(model.layers[2].output_shape)  # Dense(10)
exercise.explain: Layer by layer. LSTM(64, return_sequences=True) emits its 64-dimensional hidden state at every timestep: (None, 20, 64) — the time axis survives. LSTM(32) defaults to return_sequences=False, so it collapses the sequence to the last timestep's hidden state: (None, 32). Dense(10) remaps only the last axis, 32 to 10: (None, 10) — one logit vector per sequence, which is what sequence classification wants. A forgets that return_sequences=True keeps the time axis — and without it the second LSTM would crash at build time, because it demands a 3-D sequence input; B keeps the time axis through everything, forgetting that the final LSTM collapses it by default (a Dense applied to (None, 20, 32) really would give (None, 20, 10) — one prediction per timestep, the shape you want for sequence labeling, not classification); D mixes the two confusions.
